drills.los_text: describe the roles of equities in the overall portfolio

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely one of the primary roles equities play in an overall portfolio?

options.B: Guaranteed principal protection.
options.C: Capital appreciation.

rationales.A: Dividend income is one of the four primary roles. Equities distribute cash to shareholders through dividends, and that income stream can be a significant part of total return.
rationales.B: Equities do not offer guaranteed principal protection; the shareholder holds the residual claim and can lose the entire investment. The four primary roles equities play are capital appreciation, dividend income, diversification with other asset classes, and a potential hedge against inflation. Client considerations such as risk tolerance, time horizon, tax status and liquidity needs then drive how much equity exposure is appropriate.
rationales.C: Capital appreciation is one of the four primary roles, and historically the dominant driver of long-run equity returns.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities in a Portfolio

questions.stem: Across world markets over the 1900-2022 period, long-run real returns on the major asset classes most likely showed that:

options.A: Equity real returns were negative in most countries.
options.B: Bonds outperformed equities globally.
options.C: Equities outperformed both bonds and bills globally.

rationales.A: Real equity returns were positive in the large majority of markets over the period, not negative. Equities delivered the highest long-run real returns among the major asset classes across world markets.
rationales.B: This reverses the historical record: equities, not bonds, were the strongest performer. Both bonds and bills lagged equities in real terms across world markets over 1900-2022.
rationales.C: Long-term returns on equities, driven predominantly by capital appreciation, have historically been among the highest of any major asset class. Over 1900-2022 equities outperformed both bonds and bills across the world, with the world equity real return running at approximately 5.0% annualized. That realized premium over bonds and bills is the empirical basis for the capital appreciation role equities play in a portfolio.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — Exhibit 1 real returns

questions.stem: Capital appreciation in an equity portfolio is most likely to arise in:

options.A: Companies with growth in earnings, cash flows, or revenues.
options.B: Companies with declining earnings, cash flows, or revenues.
options.C: Mature dividend-paying companies only.

rationales.A: Capital appreciation occurs when investing in companies with growth in earnings, cash flows and/or revenues, as well as in companies with competitive success. It can be found in growth-oriented companies such as small technology firms and equally in large, mature companies where management successfully maintains profitability. Equities also tend to outperform during periods of strong economic growth, when that earnings and revenue growth is most widely available.
rationales.B: Declining earnings, cash flows or revenues typically depress a share price rather than cause it to appreciate, because deteriorating fundamentals reduce the value of the residual claim held by shareholders.
rationales.C: Restricting appreciation to mature dividend-paying companies is too narrow. Growth-oriented small technology companies are an explicitly identified source of capital appreciation, alongside large mature companies whose management sustains profitability.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — capital appreciation

questions.stem: Since 1990, the dividend yield on the S&P 500 has most likely been in the range of:

rationales.A: A yield of 8% to 10% is far above anything the S&P 500 has offered since 1990; sustaining it would require either extraordinary payout ratios or a collapse in index prices.
rationales.B: Since 1990 the dividend yield on the S&P 500 has been in the 1% to 3% range. Even at that level the effect of dividends can be significant during periods of weak equity market performance, such as the first decade of the 21st century, when index price returns were negative and dividends supplied essentially all of the total return. Dividend yield also varies considerably by sector, with utilities and consumer staples typically yielding well above the index and technology well below it.
rationales.C: A yield of 4% to 7% overstates the post-1990 range. Yields of that order characterize earlier decades, with their higher payout ratios and lower valuations, rather than the period since 1990.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — S&P 500 dividend yield range

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a source of dividend income for equity portfolios?

options.B: Interest payments on the company's bonds.
options.C: Special dividends and optional stock dividends.

rationales.A: Regular dividends on common stock are the primary source of dividend income for an equity portfolio.
rationales.B: Interest paid on a company's bonds is income to the bondholders, not to the equity holders. It is a contractual expense of the issuer that ranks ahead of any distribution to shareholders. The sources of dividend income for equity portfolios are regular dividends on common stock, preferred dividends for preferred shareholders, special dividends paid when a company distributes excess cash, and optional stock dividends, where shareholders elect either cash or new shares and the optionality itself has value.
rationales.C: Special dividends, paid when a company distributes excess cash, and optional stock dividends are both recognized sources of dividend income for equity portfolios.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — dividend sources

questions.stem: A caveat to the diversification benefit of combining equities with other asset classes is most likely that:

options.A: correlations rise across asset classes during market crises.
options.B: diversification benefits hold regardless of market conditions.
options.C: correlations are stable across time and market environments.

rationales.A: Correlations are not constant over time. Over a long historical period the correlation between two asset classes may be low, but in any given sub-period it can differ materially from that long-term average. During periods of market crisis, correlations across asset classes, and among equities themselves, often increase, which reduces the diversification benefit at exactly the moment it is most needed. The volatility of asset class returns also varies over time, so both inputs to a diversification estimate are unstable.
rationales.B: Diversification benefits are not guaranteed across market conditions. They weaken precisely when they are most needed, because crisis-period correlations across asset classes and among individual equities move toward one.
rationales.C: Correlations are not stable across time or market environments; they shift with the regime. A low long-run average correlation can coexist with sharply higher correlations during a stressed sub-period, and realized volatility shifts with it.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — diversification caveats

questions.stem: The effectiveness of equities as an inflation hedge is most likely:

options.B: reliable in all inflationary regimes.
options.C: uniformly negative.

rationales.A: Real equity returns and inflation have a positive correlation over the long term, but the degree of that correlation varies by country and by time period. For severe inflationary periods, with an annual inflation rate above about 5%, studies have shown real returns on equities and inflation to be negatively correlated, so the asset class's efficacy as an inflation hedge may fail when it is most needed. Some issuers hedge better than others: broad commodity producers benefit directly from rising commodity prices, and companies able to pass higher input costs through to customers protect their margins. Taken as a whole, the empirical evidence is mixed and the hedging ability varies by sector and by company.
rationales.B: Equities are not a reliable hedge under all inflationary regimes. The empirical evidence is mixed rather than confirmatory, and in severe inflationary periods, above roughly 5% annually, the measured relationship between real equity returns and inflation has been negative.
rationales.C: The relationship is not uniformly negative. Over long horizons real equity returns and inflation are positively correlated; it is only in severe inflationary episodes, above about 5% annually, that the correlation has turned negative.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — inflation hedge

questions.stem: The investment objectives and constraints considered in including equities in a client's portfolio are least likely to include:

options.B: a liquidity requirement.
options.C: legal and regulatory factors.

rationales.A: A brokerage account's trading commission tier is an implementation cost, not one of the seven objectives and constraints. The seven are: (1) risk objective, (2) return objective, (3) liquidity requirement, (4) time horizon, (5) tax concerns, (6) legal and regulatory factors, and (7) unique circumstances, which may include ESG issues or religious preferences.
rationales.B: The liquidity requirement is the third of the seven considerations, alongside the risk objective, the return objective, the time horizon, tax concerns, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances.
rationales.C: Legal and regulatory factors are the sixth of the seven considerations, alongside the risk objective, the return objective, the liquidity requirement, the time horizon, tax concerns, and unique circumstances.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — IPS considerations

questions.stem: Historically, the ESG approaches used by portfolio managers have most likely consisted primarily of:

options.B: negative and positive screening.
options.C: activist investing.

rationales.A: Factor investing is a separate concept. A purely quantitative factor process is not what ESG practice has historically consisted of, and a factor tilt does not by itself exclude or favor companies on environmental, social, or governance grounds.
rationales.B: Historically, ESG approaches have largely represented negative screening, which excludes certain sectors or companies that deviate from accepted standards, and positive or best-in-class screening, which identifies companies scoring most favorably on ESG risks and opportunities. Negative screening might exclude oil and gas producers from the investable universe; positive screening might overweight companies with strong governance practices, such as an independent board chair.
rationales.C: Activist investing is a separate concept. Engaging management or pressing for change at a holding is one route to influencing ESG outcomes, but it was not the dominant historical approach; screening was.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — ESG approaches historically

questions.stem: As of 2020, the largest sustainable investment strategy globally is most likely:

options.B: Positive screening.
options.C: ESG integration.

rationales.A: Negative, or exclusionary, screening was the historical approach and remains widely used, but as of 2020 it was no longer the largest sustainable investment strategy globally.
rationales.B: Positive, or best-in-class, screening is smaller than ESG integration. Like negative screening, it belongs to the earlier screening generation of approaches rather than the largest current one.
rationales.C: Rather than screening, as of 2020 the largest sustainable investment strategy globally was ESG integration, the inclusion of ESG considerations in financial analysis and investment decisions. The goals of ESG integration are to reduce financial risks and enhance financial returns by identifying and valuing risks or opportunities that are not typically identified and valued.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — ESG integration

questions.stem: A risk-averse and conservative equity investor's preferences most likely align with:

options.B: Established companies with stable cash flow and meaningful dividends.
options.C: Highly volatile emerging market equities.

rationales.A: Smaller companies with greater growth potential suit a growth-oriented investor with aggressive risk tolerance, because they carry higher return volatility than a risk-averse and conservative investor typically prefers.
rationales.B: A risk-averse and conservative investor may prefer some exposure to well-established companies with strong and stable cash flow that pay meaningful dividends. Conversely, a growth-oriented investor with aggressive risk tolerance may prefer smaller companies with greater growth potential. Portfolio managers can adapt specific factors, such as growth potential, income generation, risk and return volatility, and macroeconomic sensitivity, to an investor's goals and tolerance.
rationales.C: High volatility is inconsistent with risk aversion. Emerging market equities add currency, political, and liquidity risk on top of equity risk, which cuts against a conservative investor's preference for stable cash flow and dividend income.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — client considerations

questions.stem: Preserving the purchasing power of a client's portfolio during inflation is most likely accomplished by holding:

options.A: companies with pricing power and commodity producers.
options.B: cash equivalents only.
options.C: long-duration nominal bonds.

rationales.A: Companies successful at passing along higher input costs, such as raw materials, energy, and wages, to their customers can protect their margins as prices rise. Commodity producers in oil or industrial metals benefit directly from rising commodity prices. Certain sectors therefore provide some inflation protection, while recognizing that the equity asset class overall is mixed at best as an inflation hedge: in severe inflationary periods real equity returns and inflation have been negatively correlated.
rationales.B: Cash equivalents lose purchasing power as prices rise, since their nominal yield typically lags realized inflation. The equity answer is companies with pricing power and commodity producers.
rationales.C: Long-duration nominal bonds are among the assets most damaged by inflation. Their fixed coupons are fixed in nominal terms, and their long duration magnifies the price loss when inflation pushes nominal yields higher.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Roles of Equities — inflation hedge, Huber example

drills.los_text: describe how an equity manager's investment universe can be segmented

questions.stem: The three primary approaches to segmenting the equity investment universe are most likely:

options.B: large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap.
options.C: growth, value, and blend.

rationales.A: The three primary segmentation approaches are (1) size and style, (2) geography, and (3) economic activity, such as sector or industry. Each has its own advantages and disadvantages, and they can be combined: the MSCI Europe Large Cap Growth Index, for instance, combines geography, size, and style.
rationales.B: These are size categories, and size is only one axis within a single segmentation approach, size and style. They say nothing about geography or economic activity.
rationales.C: These are style dimensions, and style is only one axis within a single segmentation approach, size and style. They say nothing about geography or economic activity.

questions.stem: In size/style segmentation, style is most likely determined by:

options.A: a composite score built from several valuation and growth ratios.
options.B: market capitalization alone.
options.C: the company's geographic domicile.

rationales.A: Style is often determined through a scoring system that incorporates multiple metrics or ratios, such as price-to-book, price-to-earnings, earnings growth, dividend yield, and book value growth. These metrics are scored individually for each company, assigned weights, and aggregated into a composite score that determines where the stock falls along the value-growth spectrum. A combination of growth and value is not uncommon, particularly for large corporations with both mature and higher-growth business lines.
rationales.B: Market capitalization defines the size axis of size/style segmentation. Determining style requires valuation and growth inputs such as price-to-book, price-to-earnings, earnings growth, dividend yield, and book value growth.
rationales.C: Domicile is the basis of the geographic segmentation approach, not of style. Style scoring blends price-to-book, price-to-earnings, earnings growth, dividend yield, and book value growth into a composite along the value-growth spectrum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely an advantage of segmenting the equity universe by size and style?

options.A: Diversification across economic sectors or industries.
options.B: Stability of size/style classifications over time.
options.C: Straightforward portfolio construction reflecting desired risk, return, and income.

rationales.A: This is one of the four advantages: size and style segments draw on companies from across economic sectors and industries, so a portfolio built from them is diversified by sector rather than concentrated in one.
rationales.B: Stability is a disadvantage of size/style segmentation, not an advantage: the categories may change over time, and they may be defined differently among investors. The four advantages are (1) straightforward portfolio construction reflecting desired risk, return, and income characteristics, (2) diversification across sectors and industries, (3) the ability to construct performance benchmarks for specific size/style segments, and (4) accommodation of a company's maturity and changing growth or value orientation, as when a company moves from small-cap growth at its initial public offering to mature large-cap value.
rationales.C: This is one of the four advantages: the size and style axes map directly onto the risk, return, and income characteristics an investor wants, so a portfolio reflecting those characteristics can be assembled in a straightforward manner.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation by Size and Style — advantages/disadvantages

questions.stem: A small technology company that has just completed an IPO is most likely classified as:

options.B: Small cap growth, with later migration in size and style.
options.C: Large cap value.

rationales.A: Classification is not permanent. Companies migrate along the size and style spectrum: an issuer that grows successfully moves from small cap into mid cap and then large cap, and its style can shift from high growth toward value or toward a growth-and-income blend. Treating the small-cap growth label as fixed for the whole life cycle ignores that migration.
rationales.B: Many companies that undertake an IPO are small and in a growth phase, so they initially fall into the small-cap growth category. If they grow successfully, their size classification may move to mid cap or large cap, while their style may shift from high growth to value or to a combination of growth and income. Over the life cycle, investor preferences tend to shift from capital appreciation toward dividend income, which is what pulls the style label away from pure growth.
rationales.C: A newly listed technology company is small by market capitalization and is valued on expected earnings growth rather than on current fundamentals, so neither the large-cap nor the value label fits at the time of the IPO. Large cap value sits at the opposite end of both the size and the style axis, and is at most where such a company might arrive many years later, after it has grown and matured.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation by Size and Style — company life cycle

questions.stem: Under geographic segmentation of equity markets, the categories used are most likely:

options.B: Developed, emerging, and frontier markets.
options.C: Developed markets only.

rationales.A: These are broad geographic regions rather than the market tiers used to segment global equity markets. Regional labels say nothing about a market's level of economic development, its size and liquidity, or its accessibility to foreign investors, which are the criteria the tier classification is built on, and they leave frontier markets without a place of their own.
rationales.B: The common geographic categories are developed markets, emerging markets, and frontier markets. MSCI classifies countries using a holistic framework that considers economic development, market size and liquidity, and accessibility criteria such as openness to foreign equity ownership. FTSE, S&P, and Russell publish similar classifications and similar index families, with broadly comparable, though not identical, country assignments.
rationales.C: Developed markets are one tier of three. Emerging markets and frontier markets are separate categories, distinguished by lower levels of economic development, smaller size and thinner liquidity, and more restricted accessibility for foreign investors. Stopping at developed markets would leave most of the investable universe outside North America, Western Europe, and developed Asia-Pacific unclassified.

questions.stem: A key weakness of geographic segmentation of equity markets is most likely that:

options.A: investing in a specific market may give lower-than-expected exposure to it.
options.B: geographic indexes perfectly represent local economic activity.
options.C: currency risk is eliminated.

rationales.A: An index named after a country can deliver far less exposure to that country's economy than its name suggests. Nestle, Roche, and Novartis together account for over half of the MSCI Switzerland Index, yet Switzerland accounts for less than 2% of each company's sales, so what looks like Swiss equity exposure is largely exposure to global multinationals. A second weakness of the approach is the currency risk taken on when investing across global equity markets.
rationales.B: This reverses the weakness. Geographic indexes are often not representative of the local economy, because they are dominated by large multinationals that earn their revenues abroad: more than half of the MSCI Switzerland Index sits in Nestle, Roche, and Novartis, each of which generates under 2% of sales in Switzerland. Perfect representation would in any case be a strength rather than a weakness.
rationales.C: Currency risk is introduced by investing across geographic markets, not eliminated by them. The return on a foreign equity holding combines the local-market return with the move in the exchange rate, and that currency exposure has to be hedged deliberately if it is unwanted. Dividing the opportunity set by geography does nothing to remove it.

questions.stem: Of the following pairs, the pair least likely to be among the primary commercial global systems for classifying companies by economic activity is:

options.A: Thomson Reuters Business Classification and Russell Global Sectors.
options.B: Standard Industrial Classification and North American Industry Classification System.
options.C: Global Industry Classification Standard and Industrial Classification Benchmark.

rationales.A: The Thomson Reuters Business Classification and the Russell Global Sectors Classification are two of the four primary commercial global systems, alongside the Global Industry Classification Standard and the Industrial Classification Benchmark.
rationales.B: The Standard Industrial Classification and the North American Industry Classification System are US government statistical classifications, used for official economic reporting rather than for index construction, so they are not among the primary commercial global systems. Those four are the Global Industry Classification Standard, the Industrial Classification Benchmark, the Thomson Reuters Business Classification, and the Russell Global Sectors Classification.
rationales.C: The Global Industry Classification Standard and the Industrial Classification Benchmark are the two best known of the four primary commercial global systems; the remaining two are the Thomson Reuters Business Classification and the Russell Global Sectors Classification.

questions.stem: The levels of the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) hierarchy are most likely:

options.B: 11 sectors, 24 industry groups, 68 industries, and 157 sub-industries.
options.C: 20 sectors, 40 industry groups, 100 industries, and 300 sub-industries.

rationales.A: These counts are too low at every level. GICS runs 11 sectors, 24 industry groups, 68 industries, and 157 sub-industries, so a five-sector top level would have to collapse distinctions such as energy, materials, utilities, and real estate into one another.
rationales.B: GICS has four levels: 11 sectors at the first level, 24 industry groups at the second, 68 industries at the third, and 157 sub-industries at the fourth. A company is assigned a single code at the most granular level, and the chain runs upward from there. For example, the motorcycle manufacturers sub-industry sits within the automobiles industry, which sits within the automobiles and components industry group, which sits within the consumer discretionary sector.
rationales.C: These counts are too high at every level. GICS has 11 sectors rather than 20, and 24 industry groups, 68 industries, and 157 sub-industries rather than 40, 100, and 300.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation by Economic Activity — GICS structure

questions.stem: The levels of the Industrial Classification Benchmark (ICB) hierarchy are most likely:

options.A: 10 industries, 19 super sectors, 41 sectors, and 114 sub-sectors.
options.B: 11 sectors, 24 industry groups, 68 industries, and 157 sub-industries.
options.C: 10 sectors, 40 industries, and 100 sub-sectors.

rationales.A: ICB has four levels: 10 industries at the first level, 19 super sectors at the second, 41 sectors at the third, and 114 sub-sectors at the fourth. The terminology is the trap when systems are compared. ICB uses industries at its highest level, where GICS uses sectors, and ICB then uses sectors at its third level, so the same word denotes a different level of granularity in each system.
rationales.B: These are the GICS counts: 11 sectors, 24 industry groups, 68 industries, and 157 sub-industries. ICB is both coarser and differently named, with 10 industries, 19 super sectors, 41 sectors, and 114 sub-sectors.
rationales.C: ICB has four levels rather than three, and none of these counts matches it. Its hierarchy is 10 industries, 19 super sectors, 41 sectors, and 114 sub-sectors, and its top level is labeled industries rather than sectors.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation by Economic Activity — ICB structure

questions.stem: A key disadvantage of segmentation by economic activity is most likely that:

options.A: a company's activities may span more than one industry.
options.B: the classifications are excessively standardized.
options.C: the classifications are updated too infrequently.

rationales.A: The business activities of companies, particularly large ones, may include more than one industry or sub-industry, so a single classification code does not fully capture a diversified group. A multinational conglomerate can operate across several sectors while being assigned to just one, which distorts the sector weights of an index and any attribution built on them.
rationales.B: Standardization is an advantage of these systems rather than a disadvantage. A common framework applied consistently across providers, markets, and time is what makes sector comparisons and peer groups possible in the first place. The weakness lies elsewhere: a single code cannot represent a company whose activities span several industries.
rationales.C: Update frequency is not the disadvantage at issue. Providers do reassign companies as their business mixes change. The structural problem is that a diversified company, especially a large conglomerate, operates in more than one industry or sub-industry at any given moment, so no single code, however recently reviewed, captures it.

questions.stem: A manager is launching a fund that invests in Chinese robotics companies with rapidly accelerating earnings. The fund's equity universe is most appropriately segmented by:

options.B: economic activity alone.
options.C: size and style, with a growth orientation.

rationales.A: Geography is already fixed by the mandate: every candidate holding is Chinese, so segmenting by geography separates nothing within the universe and adds no discriminating power. That dimension would matter only to a fund choosing among markets.
rationales.B: Segmentation by economic activity is equally uninformative here, because the mandate also fixes the industry: the candidates are all robotics companies, with similar industry composition. It says nothing about the characteristic the strategy is built on, which is the pace of earnings growth. Size and style segmentation with a growth orientation does capture that characteristic.
rationales.C: Given a strategy of investing in companies with rapidly accelerating earnings, the manager would most likely segment by size and style, using a style that reflects growth, with the size dimension, large, mid, or small cap, depending on the companies selected. Geographic and economic activity segmentation are both less appropriate, because the geographic and industry composition of the target universe is already uniform and neither dimension distinguishes one candidate from another.

questions.stem: An equity index most likely to reflect a combination of geographic, size, and style segmentation is:

options.A: The MSCI Europe Large Cap Growth Index.
options.B: The Dow Jones Industrial Average.
options.C: The S&P 500.

rationales.A: The name carries all three dimensions at once: Europe is the geographic segment, large cap the size segment, and growth the style segment. Indexes built the same way include the MSCI World Small Cap Value Index, the MSCI Emerging Markets Large Cap Growth Index, and the MSCI Latin America Midcap Index. The combination is also applied within individual countries, particularly large developed markets.
rationales.B: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a 30-stock price-weighted index of large US companies selected by a committee, so it applies neither a size screen nor a style screen on top of its geographic scope. The indexes that do combine the dimensions are named for them, such as MSCI Europe Large Cap Growth and MSCI World Small Cap Value, which blend geography, size, and style.
rationales.C: The S&P 500 reflects a single approach: a selective large-cap US universe chosen by a committee, with no style dimension applied to it. Style sub-indexes such as S&P 500 Growth and S&P 500 Value are derived from it, but the parent index itself is not an example of a combined-approach index.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation of Equity Indexes and Benchmarks

questions.stem: The geographic scope of equity indexes defined by economic sector is most likely:

options.B: multi-country for whole markets but not for individual sectors.
options.C: frequently global, spanning companies in many countries.

rationales.A: Sector indexes routinely cross borders, because many sectors are themselves global. Examples include the S&P Global Natural Resources Index, the MSCI World Energy Index, and the Refinitiv Global Financials Index, none of which is confined to a single country.
rationales.B: Multi-country construction is not reserved for whole-market indexes. Sector indexes are built across countries as well: the S&P Global Natural Resources Index holds the 90 largest publicly traded natural resources and commodities companies, spanning agribusiness, energy, and metals and mining worldwide.
rationales.C: Because many sectors are global in nature, industry-focused indexes are often global in scope. Examples include the S&P Global Natural Resources Index, covering the 90 largest publicly traded companies in natural resources and commodities across agribusiness, energy, and metals and mining; the MSCI World Energy Index, covering the large-cap and mid-cap segments of publicly traded oil and natural gas companies in developed markets; and the Refinitiv Global Financials Index, covering the 100 largest global financial services companies.

questions.curriculum_ref: Segmentation of Equity Indexes — sector indexes

drills.los_text: describe the types of income and costs associated with owning and managing an equity portfolio and their potential effects on portfolio performance

questions.stem: The primary source of income for an equity portfolio is most likely:

options.B: Capital gains.
options.C: Bond interest.

rationales.A: Dividends, both regular and special, are the primary source of income for equity portfolios. Beyond regular dividends, a portfolio may receive special dividends, paid when a company distributes excess cash, and optional stock dividends, where the shareholder elects either cash or new shares. That dividend income is then supplemented by securities lending fees and interest, by dividend-capture strategies, and by option premiums from writing covered calls and cash-covered puts.
rationales.B: Capital gains on trades are price appreciation realized on disposal, not income. They are a component of total return, but they sit outside the income component, which is built on dividends and supplemented by securities lending fees, dividend capture, and option premiums.
rationales.C: Interest on bond holdings is the primary income source of a fixed-income portfolio, not of an equity portfolio. An equity mandate holds little or no debt, and its income comes from dividends, supplemented by securities lending fees, dividend capture, and option writing.

questions.curriculum_ref: Income Associated with Owning and Managing an Equity Portfolio

questions.stem: Securities lending fees for stock loans in developed markets on typical shares are most likely:

options.B: 5%–10% annualized.
options.C: 25%–100% annualized.

rationales.A: Most stock loans in developed markets earn a modest fee, approximately 0.2%–0.5% on an annualized basis. In emerging markets, fees are typically higher, often 1%–2% annualized for large-cap stocks. Certain shares in high demand for borrowing, known as 'specials', can earn substantially higher fees of 5%–15% annualized, or 25%–100% in conditions of extreme demand, but such high fees do not normally persist for long.
rationales.B: A fee of 5%–10% annualized is in the range earned by 'specials' — shares in high demand for borrowing — rather than by typical developed market shares, which earn roughly 0.2%–0.5% annualized. Even for specials, fees at that level tend not to persist.
rationales.C: A fee of 25%–100% annualized is the extreme-demand range for scarce 'specials', and it is short-lived. Typical developed market loans earn roughly 0.2%–0.5% annualized, and emerging market large-cap loans around 1%–2%.

questions.curriculum_ref: Securities Lending Income — DM fee ranges

questions.stem: When a stock is loaned out, the dividends paid on that stock are most likely:

options.A: Manufactured by the borrower for the lender.
options.B: Kept by the borrower, with no compensation to the lender.
options.C: Cancelled for the duration of the loan.

rationales.A: Dividends on loaned stock are 'manufactured' by the stock borrower for the stock lender: the borrower ensures that the lender is compensated for any dividends the lender would have received had the stock not been loaned. The lender's economic dividend income is therefore preserved intact, and the securities lending fee is incremental income on top of it.
rationales.B: The borrower does not simply keep the dividend. Because legal title passes with the loan, the issuer's dividend reaches the holder of record, but the borrower then manufactures an equivalent payment to the lender, so the lender is compensated rather than left out of pocket.
rationales.C: A stock loan does not cancel or suspend dividends on the shares. The issuer continues to pay as normal; the dividend simply reaches the lender indirectly, manufactured by the borrower.

questions.stem: Index funds are frequent lenders of stock most likely because of:

options.B: Large, long-term holdings and indifference to short-sale price pressure.
options.C: A need for external cash to fund operations.

rationales.A: No regulation requires an index fund to lend its shares. Lending is a commercial decision taken to add income, and a fund is free to decline to lend or to recall loaned stock.
rationales.B: Index funds are frequent stock lenders because of their large, long-term holdings in stocks, and because index-fund managers are normally not concerned that borrowed stock used for short-selling purposes might decrease the prices of the corresponding equities — the fund merely seeks to replicate the performance of an index rather than to express a view on price. Large actively managed pension funds, endowments, and institutional investors are also frequent lenders, though they tend to be more concerned about the price impact of short selling.
rationales.C: Operational cash is not the driver. The attraction of lending is incremental income on a large, stable, long-term holding, combined with the manager's indifference to any price pressure the borrowed stock may create through short selling.

questions.curriculum_ref: Securities Lending — index funds as lenders

questions.stem: The dividend capture strategy is most likely described as:

options.A: Holding stocks indefinitely to collect all future dividends.
options.B: Selling shares before the ex-dividend date to avoid tax.
options.C: Buying shares just before the ex-dividend date and selling after it.

rationales.A: Holding indefinitely describes a buy-and-hold approach, not dividend capture. Dividend capture is deliberately short-dated: the shares are bought shortly before the ex-dividend date and sold once the right to the dividend has been earned.
rationales.B: Selling before the ex-dividend date forgoes the dividend entirely, which is the opposite of dividend capture. The strategy requires holding through the ex-dividend date precisely in order to earn the dividend right.
rationales.C: Dividend capture is purchasing stocks just before their ex-dividend dates, holding through the ex-dividend date to earn the dividend right, and subsequently selling the shares. In theory, the share price should decrease by the value of the dividend once the stock goes ex-dividend, so capturing dividends increases portfolio income while the portfolio in theory experiences capital losses of similar magnitude. Actual share price movement may vary from theory because of income tax considerations, stock-specific supply and demand, and general market moves around the ex-dividend date.

questions.stem: Writing a covered call generates income and most likely:

options.B: Limits upside from share price appreciation.
options.C: Eliminates downside risk entirely.

rationales.A: Upside participation is not left unlimited. The written call is covered by stock the manager already owns, so once the stock trades above the strike the shares are called away and any further appreciation accrues to the option buyer rather than the portfolio.
rationales.B: In a covered call the portfolio manager owns the underlying stock and sells a call option on it. The option premium generates income, but the risk profile is clearly altered: writing the covered call limits the upside from share price appreciation of the underlying shares, because if the stock rises above the strike the shares are called away at the strike price. The premium received is the compensation for surrendering that appreciation. A cash-covered put generates income in a similar way, with the writer required to deposit cash equal to the exercise price.
rationales.C: Downside risk is not eliminated. The manager continues to hold the shares and bears their decline in full; the call premium cushions the loss only to the extent of the premium received.

questions.stem: Management fees for equity portfolios are most likely determined as:

options.A: A fixed amount independent of portfolio value.
options.B: A percentage of the funds under management.
options.C: A percentage of realized capital gains only.

rationales.A: A fee fixed in money terms, unresponsive to the value of the portfolio, is not the typical arrangement for an equity portfolio. Fees are charged ad valorem, so that the manager's revenue scales with the assets under management.
rationales.B: Management fees are typically determined as a percentage of the funds under management, an ad-valorem fee, charged at regular intervals. For actively managed portfolios, the fee must balance being high enough to fund research and low enough not to detract too much from returns; it covers the direct costs of research, including analyst and portfolio manager remuneration and expenses, and of portfolio management, including software, trade processing, and compliance. Index-based management fees are typically low, reflecting the lower direct research and portfolio management costs of replication.
rationales.C: A charge levied on realized capital gains alone describes a performance, or incentive, fee. That is distinct from the ad-valorem management fee and is generally associated with hedge funds and long/short portfolios.

questions.stem: Performance fees in equity portfolios are most likely:

options.A: Waived on all hedge fund performance.
options.B: Associated with hedge funds rather than long-only portfolios.
options.C: Identical to management fees and paid regardless of returns.

rationales.A: Performance fees are not waived. They are earned and collected when the stated performance objective is met, and they tend to be 'upwards only': charged when objectives are met, but not reimbursed when performance is negative, though they can be reduced following poor performance.
rationales.B: Performance fees, also called incentive fees, are generally associated with hedge funds and long/short equity portfolios rather than with long-only portfolios. A typical structure is 10%–20% of any capital appreciation above a stated annual absolute return threshold, for example 8%. Such fees tend to be 'upwards only' — earned when performance objectives are met but not reimbursed when performance is negative, although they can be reduced following poor performance. The calculation also reflects a high-water mark, the highest value net of fees that the fund has reached, which protects the client from paying twice for the same performance.
rationales.C: A performance fee is distinct from a management fee. The management fee is ad valorem and charged at regular intervals whatever the return, whereas the performance fee is contingent: charged on appreciation above a stated threshold and subject to a high-water mark.

questions.stem: For a client paying performance fees, the benefit of a high-water mark is most likely:

options.A: Avoiding a second fee on the same performance.
options.B: Avoiding management fees altogether.
options.C: Avoiding regulatory penalties.

rationales.A: The high-water mark, the highest value net of fees that the fund has reached, protects the client from paying twice for the same performance. If a fund performs well in its first year, a performance fee is earned. If the fund's value then falls the following year, no performance fee is payable. If the value increases in the third year to a point just below the value achieved at the end of the first year, no performance fee is earned in that year either, because the fund's value did not exceed the high-water mark. This basic structure is used by many alternative investment funds and partnerships, including hedge funds.
rationales.B: Management fees are unaffected by a high-water mark. The ad-valorem management fee continues to be charged at regular intervals on the funds under management whatever the performance; the high-water mark constrains only the performance fee.
rationales.C: A high-water mark is a contractual feature of the fee calculation agreed with investors, not a regulatory protection, and it does nothing to shield a client from penalties.

questions.stem: A component of the trading costs borne by an equity portfolio is least likely:

options.B: Delay costs, or slippage.
options.C: Performance-fee accruals.

rationales.A: Explicit costs and implicit costs are two of the three components of trading cost. Explicit costs are commissions, fees, and taxes; implicit costs are the bid-ask spread and market impact, the effect a trade itself has on transaction prices.
rationales.B: Delay costs, also called slippage, are the third component of trading cost. They arise from the inability to complete the desired trades immediately, because of the size of the order or a lack of market liquidity.
rationales.C: Performance-fee accruals are a portfolio management cost charged by the manager, not a cost of trading. The three components of trading cost are explicit costs (commissions, fees, and taxes), implicit costs (the bid-ask spread and market impact, the effect of a trade on transaction prices), and delay costs or slippage (the inability to complete desired trades immediately because of order size or lack of market liquidity).

questions.stem: Compared with management fees, the total cost of trading an equity portfolio is most likely:

options.B: itemized in quarterly investor reports.
options.C: embedded in reported total return.

rationales.A: Trading costs are not always larger than management fees; their relative size varies with portfolio turnover, the strategy being run and the fee schedule, and for a low-turnover mandate the management fee usually dominates. The distinguishing feature of trading costs is not their size but their visibility.
rationales.B: Itemized periodic disclosure of the total cost of trading is not standard practice. Management fees are explicit and reported, but the components of trading cost — commissions, bid–ask spreads, market impact and delay cost — are absorbed into the portfolio's returns rather than reported line by line to investors.
rationales.C: Unlike many other equity portfolio costs such as management fees, the total cost of trading is generally not revealed to the investor. Trading costs are instead incorporated into a portfolio's total return and presented as overall performance data. That treatment makes them far less visible than explicit fee items, and harder for an investor to monitor, compare across managers or control.

questions.stem: For an index fund, the most significant hidden cost is most likely:

options.A: a commission premium over active managers.
options.B: none, given low turnover and transparency.
options.C: predatory trading around index changes.

rationales.A: Index funds generally pay lower commissions than active funds, not higher: they trade less often and can work orders patiently around known rebalance dates, and their scale gives them negotiating power on rates. The hidden cost is predatory trading ahead of announced inclusions and deletions, not a commission premium.
rationales.B: Transparency is the vulnerability here rather than a protection. Because index membership changes are announced in advance and the fund must hold the index weights by the effective date, its trades are predictable in both direction and timing, and predictable trades invite predation. Low turnover reduces how often the cost is incurred, not whether it exists.
rationales.C: Index funds face a hidden cost from potential predatory trading. A predatory trader may purchase (or sell short) shares prior to their effective inclusion in (or deletion from) an index, moving the price against the index fund and generating a profit for the predator. Such strategies are a real cost to index fund investors — albeit a cost that is not necessarily evident to the portfolio manager or the investor, because it surfaces only as a worse execution price rather than as a reported charge.

questions.curriculum_ref: Investment Approaches and Effects on Costs — predatory trading

questions.stem: Relative to a deep value strategy, a momentum strategy most likely has:

options.B: higher trading costs.
options.C: lower trading costs.

rationales.A: The two strategies take fundamentally different liquidity postures, so their trading costs differ. Dealing in the same universe of listed equities, through the same brokers and venues, does not equalize cost: what drives cost is whether the strategy must pay up to get filled or can wait to be filled.
rationales.B: Some active investing approaches demand liquidity from the market. In a momentum strategy the investor seeks to buy shares already rising in price, or to sell those already falling, which means taking the price the other side is offering in order to get the trade done, and doing so frequently. Deep value strategies, which buy stocks deemed significantly undervalued, are more likely to provide liquidity to the market, supplying the other side of trades that others need done. Strategies that trade frequently and demand liquidity are, unsurprisingly, likely to have higher trading costs than long-term, buy-and-hold strategies.
rationales.C: The relationship runs the other way. Momentum demands liquidity by chasing what is already moving, while patient value buying tends to supply it: the deep value manager normally chooses when to trade and can bid passively, often being paid the spread rather than paying it. Wider quoted spreads on unloved names therefore do not dominate, because the value manager is under no obligation to cross them.

drills.los_text: describe the potential benefits of shareholder engagement and the role an equity manager might play in shareholder engagement

questions.stem: Shareholder engagement is most likely defined as:

options.A: active interaction between investors and companies.
options.B: the buying and selling of shares in secondary markets.
options.C: passive index investing with no company contact.

rationales.A: Shareholder engagement is the process whereby investors actively interact with companies. It often includes voting on corporate matters at general meetings as well as other forms of communication, such as quarterly investor calls and in-person meetings with management. Engagement generally concerns issues that can affect the value of a company and, by extension, the value of an investor's shares.
rationales.B: Buying and selling shares is portfolio management, and it is transacted with other market participants rather than with the company itself. Engagement is interaction with the company — voting at general meetings, investor calls, meetings with management — on matters that bear on company value.
rationales.C: Passivity in trading neither precludes engagement nor constitutes it. A manager who never trades can still vote its proxies and meet management, and a manager who trades constantly may never speak to a company. Engagement is defined by the interaction with the company, not by the turnover of the portfolio.

questions.stem: A common topic of shareholder engagement is least likely to be:

options.B: capital allocation, governance, remuneration, and board composition.
options.C: the firm's daily proprietary trading decisions.

rationales.A: Strategy is one of the five common engagement topics. It covers a company's goals, the resources available to it, its plans for growth, its research and development, its culture and its approach to sustainability.
rationales.B: These are the other four of the five common topics: allocation of capital (dividends, financial leverage, equity raising and capital expenditure); corporate governance together with regulatory and political risk, including internal controls and the audit and risk committees; remuneration, meaning compensation structures, incentives and their alignment with shareholders; and composition of the board of directors, covering succession, expertise, culture, diversity and effectiveness.
rationales.C: A company's day-to-day dealing decisions are an operational matter for management and are not a topic of shareholder engagement, which addresses matters bearing on long-run company value. The five common topics are strategy; allocation of capital; corporate governance and regulatory or political risk; remuneration; and composition of the board of directors.

questions.stem: From a company's perspective, shareholder engagement most likely:

options.B: harms performance by distracting management.
options.C: strengthens its corporate governance culture.

rationales.A: Engagement does not remove disagreement. Shareholders and management can engage extensively and still differ over strategy, capital allocation or pay, and engagement is as likely to surface a disagreement as to settle one. The benefit to the company is a more effective governance culture, which may in turn improve performance for shareholders and other stakeholders.
rationales.B: Engagement is identified as a benefit to the company, not as a drag on its performance. It is time consuming and costly for both sides, which is listed among its disadvantages, but its effect on performance works through a strengthened governance culture and better-informed owners rather than through distraction.
rationales.C: From a company's perspective, shareholder engagement can assist in developing a more effective corporate governance culture. In turn, engagement may lead to better company performance, to the benefit of shareholders as well as other stakeholders. Investors also benefit, gaining more information about the companies they own and the sectors in which those companies operate.

questions.stem: Shareholder engagement is most likely to be relevant for:

options.B: active portfolio managers.
options.C: index-based fund managers.

rationales.A: A day trader holds positions for hours and has no interest in influencing how a company is run. Engagement requires a stake held long enough for governance or strategic change to work through into the share price, and it offers nothing to a horizon measured in minutes.
rationales.B: Shareholder engagement is particularly relevant for active portfolio managers. Engagement supplies information about a company's strategy, its culture and its competitive environment, and that information feeds directly into active investment decisions; an active manager can also size a position to benefit from the change it helps bring about, so it captures a return on the effort spent.
rationales.C: Index-based fund managers are primarily focused on tracking a benchmark while minimizing the costs of doing so, and any process such as shareholder engagement that takes up management time and adds cost detracts from that primary goal. This is less of an issue for very large index-based portfolios, where engagement costs can be spread over a sizable asset base, but the active manager remains the primary beneficiary.

questions.curriculum_ref: Benefits of Shareholder Engagement — active vs index

questions.stem: The free-rider problem in shareholder engagement is most likely:

options.B: benefit to investors who do not engage.
options.C: a regulatory requirement to engage.

rationales.A: Companies do not reimburse shareholders for the cost of engaging with them; the engaging investor bears the research time, the travel and the management attention itself. That asymmetry is precisely what creates the problem: the cost is private while the benefit is shared.
rationales.B: Investors who do not pursue engagement can still benefit from the shareholder engagement of others. If a portfolio manager using an active strategy engages with a company to improve its operations and succeeds in raising the company's stock price, the manager's actions improve the value of its own portfolio but also benefit every other holder of the same stock — none of whom incurred any of the cost of engagement. The engaging manager therefore captures only part of the return on its effort, which blunts the incentive to engage at all.
rationales.C: Compulsion is not the free-rider problem. The problem arises out of voluntary, privately funded engagement whose benefits cannot be confined to the investor who paid for them.

questions.curriculum_ref: Benefits of Shareholder Engagement — free-rider problem

questions.stem: A disadvantage of shareholder engagement is least likely to be:

options.A: pressure on management to meet near-term earnings targets.
options.B: mandatory SEC reporting of engagement discussions.
options.C: the time and cost borne by both sides.

rationales.A: This is one of the four disadvantages. Engagement can pressure management into meeting near-term share price or earnings targets at the expense of decisions that would serve the company over the long run.
rationales.B: No rule requires that engagement discussions be reported to a securities regulator. The four disadvantages are: engagement is time consuming and costly for both shareholders and companies; it can pressure management to meet near-term share price or earnings targets at the expense of long-term decisions; it risks selective disclosure of important information to a certain subset of shareholders, which could lead to a breach of insider trading rules; and it can create conflicts of interest for a company, as when a portfolio manager engages with a company that is also an investor in that manager's portfolios.
rationales.C: This is one of the four disadvantages. Engagement consumes time and money on both sides — for the shareholder who must research, prepare and conduct it, and for the company whose senior management and board must host it.

questions.stem: Activist investing is most likely described as:

options.A: engagement concerned only with executive pay.
options.B: passive index tracking without engagement.
options.C: a specialized form of engagement seeking change.

rationales.A: Remuneration is one engagement topic among several, and an activist's agenda typically runs much wider: board seats, capital allocation, divestitures and overall strategy. What defines activism is taking a stake and creating change in order to generate a gain on the investment, whichever lever is used to do it.
rationales.B: Activism is engagement intensified, not passivity. An index tracker holds benchmark weights and seeks to minimize the cost of doing so, while an activist deliberately concentrates a stake precisely in order to influence how the company is run.
rationales.C: Activist investing is a distinct and specialized version of engagement. Activists specialize in taking stakes in companies and creating change in order to generate a gain on their investment. Hedge funds are among the most common activists, possibly because of the potential for high performance fees. Because hedge funds are also subject to limited regulation, have fewer investment constraints and can often leverage positions, they tend to have more flexibility as activists than other institutional investors.

questions.stem: Beyond meetings with management, shareholder resolutions, letters to management, presentations to other investors, and media campaigns, activist investors are most likely to also seek:

options.B: board representation via proxy contests.
options.C: acquisition of all outstanding shares.

rationales.A: Activist engagement works through the people who control corporate decisions, namely senior management and the board of directors. Informal discussions with lower-level employees carry no governance leverage and are not among the engagement tools available to activists.
rationales.B: Activists may seek representation on a company's board of directors as a way of exerting influence. Proxy contests are one method used to obtain board representation: they are corporate takeover mechanisms in which shareholders are persuaded to vote for a group seeking a controlling position on a company's board of directors. Social media and other communication tools can help activists coordinate the actions of other shareholders.
rationales.C: Activist strategies rely on influencing a company while holding a minority stake, so full acquisition of the shares is not the activist's goal. Buying 100% of the equity is a takeover by an acquirer and would require committing far more capital than a typical activist position.

questions.stem: General meetings (general assemblies) are most likely important for shareholder engagement because they:

options.A: are among the most influential tools available to shareholders.
options.B: are open only to management and directors.
options.C: eliminate all shareholder rights.

rationales.A: The participation of shareholders in general meetings, also known as general assemblies, and the exercise of their voting rights are among the most influential tools available for shareholder engagement. General meetings enable shareholders to participate in discussions and to vote on major corporate matters and transactions that are not delegated to the board of directors.
rationales.B: General meetings are convened for shareholders: attendance and the exercise of voting rights are shareholder privileges, and management and directors attend in order to present to and answer to those shareholders. A meeting closed to shareholders would provide no engagement channel at all.
rationales.C: General meetings preserve shareholder rights rather than eliminate them. They are the forum in which voting rights are exercised, including votes on major corporate matters and transactions that are not delegated to the board of directors.

questions.stem: Proxy voting is most likely described as:

options.A: the automatic transfer of voting rights to the custodian holding shares in street name.
options.B: the authorization of another individual to vote on behalf of an absent shareholder.
options.C: a practice prohibited under the corporate law of most jurisdictions.

rationales.A: Voting rights are not automatically transferred to a custodian when shares are held in street name. A proxy is a person, such as another shareholder or a director, whom a shareholder unable to attend the meeting authorizes to vote on his or her behalf.
rationales.B: Proxy voting enables shareholders who are unable to attend a meeting to authorize another individual, such as another shareholder or a director, to vote on their behalf. It is the most common form of investor participation in general meetings. Although most resolutions pass without controversy, minority shareholders sometimes attempt to strengthen their influence via proxy voting, and multiple shareholders may collectively vote in favor of or in opposition to a resolution.
rationales.C: Proxy voting is standard, legally supported practice worldwide rather than a prohibited one, and it is the most common form of investor participation in general meetings.

questions.stem: External proxy advisory firms, such as Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis, most likely:

options.B: provide voting recommendations that reduce investors' research efforts.
options.C: make voting decisions binding on all shareholders.

rationales.A: Proxy advisers have no authority over a manager's votes. Portfolio managers retain voting discretion and need not follow the recommendations they receive, so the advisory relationship cannot prohibit a manager from voting.
rationales.B: Some investors use external proxy advisory firms, such as Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis, that provide voting recommendations and reduce research efforts by investors. Portfolio managers need not follow the recommendations of proxy advisers, but these external parties can highlight potentially controversial issues. An investor's voting instructions are typically processed electronically via third-party proxy voting agents.
rationales.C: These firms advise; they do not bind. Their recommendations carry no legal force over any shareholder, and each investor remains free to vote against them or to disregard them entirely.

questions.stem: When an investor loans out shares, the voting rights attached to those shares most likely:

options.A: are extinguished for the duration of the loan.
options.B: transfer to the borrower along with title.
options.C: remain with the lender throughout the loan.

rationales.A: The rights transfer rather than vanish, because a securities loan is an assignment of title and the borrower is entitled to vote the shares. A lender who wants to vote must recall the shares ahead of the voting resolution, giving up stock lending revenue for the recall period.
rationales.B: When an investor loans shares, the transaction is technically an assignment of title with a repurchase option, so voting rights are transferred to the borrower. The transfer could potentially result in the borrower having different voting opinions from the lending investor. To mitigate this, some stock lenders recall shares ahead of voting resolutions; the downside is loss of stock lending revenue during the recall period and potential reputation risk. In some cases, investors borrow shares explicitly to exercise voting rights, known as empty voting, in which no capital is invested but voting rights are acquired.
rationales.C: A securities loan transfers legal title, not merely economic exposure, and voting rights travel with title to the borrower. The lender retains the economic interest through the repurchase option but cannot vote the loaned shares unless they are recalled.
